_about: Windows event IDs for the Reference page (#events): Windows Security log events that exam objectives and SOC runbooks use most, the logon types that 4624/4625 report, and the failure status codes 4625 reports. Each event's name is Microsoft's own title, checked against its Microsoft Learn page when the entry was added (Nov 15, 2026); 'plain' and 'why' are fixed text written for the hub. Events are keyed by log and ID because IDs are only unique within one log/provider. 'page' is set when Microsoft documents the event on another event's page (domain-group events share the local-group page). Kept sorted by ID. tests/events.test.mjs checks the shape.

source.title: Microsoft Learn: Windows security auditing events

events.name: The audit log was cleared.
events.plain: Someone cleared the Windows Security log on this computer.
events.why: Attackers clear logs to hide what they did. Outside planned maintenance, treat it as a sign to investigate.

events.name: An account was successfully logged on.
events.plain: An account signed in to this computer. The logon type says how (at the keyboard, over the network, by Remote Desktop).
events.why: Many failed logons (4625) from one source followed by a 4624 can mean a password-guessing attack that worked.

events.name: An account failed to log on.
events.plain: A sign-in to this computer failed. The status code says why (no such user, wrong password, account locked).
events.why: Bursts from one source suggest password guessing; many different usernames suggest someone is checking which accounts exist.

events.name: An account was logged off.
events.plain: A logon session ended and no longer exists.
events.why: Pair it with the matching 4624 (same Logon ID) to see how long a session lasted.

events.name: User initiated logoff.
events.plain: A user chose to sign out (rather than the session simply ending).
events.why: Useful for building a timeline of who was at the keyboard and when.

events.name: A logon was attempted using explicit credentials.
events.plain: A process signed in with a username and password typed or supplied for the job, such as Run as or a mapped drive with other credentials.
events.why: Normal for admins, but from an unusual account or program it can mean stolen credentials being used to move to other machines.

events.name: Special privileges assigned to new logon.
events.plain: A new sign-in was given powerful admin-level rights (such as debugging programs or taking ownership of files).
events.why: Expected for admins and the system; for an ordinary user account it can mean privilege escalation.

events.name: A new process has been created.
events.plain: A program started. With command-line auditing on, it also records the full command that was run.
events.why: The main way to see what ran on a machine, such as encoded PowerShell or Office starting a command prompt.

events.name: A service was installed in the system.
events.plain: A new Windows service was installed.
events.why: Attackers install services to keep access or run tools with full system rights. Check any service you did not expect.

events.name: A scheduled task was created.
events.plain: A new scheduled task was added to Task Scheduler.
events.why: A common way for malware to run again after a restart. Check what the task runs and who created it.

events.name: A scheduled task was deleted.
events.plain: A scheduled task was removed.
events.why: A task created and soon deleted can be an attacker running something once and cleaning up.

events.name: A scheduled task was enabled.
events.plain: A scheduled task that was turned off was turned back on.
events.why: Watch for disabled tasks being switched back on by unexpected accounts.

events.name: A scheduled task was disabled.
events.plain: A scheduled task was turned off.
events.why: Disabling security or update tasks can be part of weakening a machine's defenses.

events.name: A scheduled task was updated.
events.plain: An existing scheduled task was changed.
events.why: Changing a trusted task to run something else is a quiet way to keep access.

events.name: System audit policy was changed.
events.plain: The settings for what Windows records in the Security log were changed.
events.why: Turning auditing off blinds defenders. Microsoft rates this event high: one occurrence is worth checking.

events.name: A user account was created.
events.plain: A new user account was created.
events.why: Attackers create accounts to keep access. Check any account nobody requested.

events.name: A user account was enabled.
events.plain: A disabled user account was turned back on.
events.why: Re-enabled old or default accounts are a common backdoor.

events.name: An attempt was made to change an account's password.
events.plain: A user tried to change their own password (it records success or failure).
events.why: Usually routine; unexpected changes on admin or service accounts are worth a look.

events.name: An attempt was made to reset an account's password.
events.plain: Someone (usually an admin) reset another account's password.
events.why: An attacker with admin rights can reset passwords to take over accounts. Check who did it.

events.name: A user account was disabled.
events.plain: A user account was turned off.
events.why: Normal when people leave; disabling many accounts at once can be sabotage.

events.name: A user account was deleted.
events.plain: A user account was deleted.
events.why: Deleting an account right after using it can be an attacker covering tracks.

events.name: A member was added to a security-enabled global group.
events.plain: An account was added to a domain (global) security group.
events.why: Additions to groups like Domain Admins give full control of the domain. Check every one.

events.name: A member was added to a security-enabled local group.
events.plain: An account was added to a security group on this computer, such as the local Administrators group.
events.why: Being added to local Administrators gives full control of that machine.

events.name: A member was removed from a security-enabled local group.
events.plain: An account was removed from a security group on this computer.
events.why: Add-then-remove in a short time can be someone borrowing admin rights and hiding it.

events.name: A user account was changed.
events.plain: Settings on a user account were changed (for example, password never expires).
events.why: Weakening settings, such as removing the need for Kerberos pre-authentication, can set up later attacks.

events.name: A user account was locked out.
events.plain: An account was locked after too many wrong passwords.
events.why: One user locked out is usually a forgotten password; many lockouts at once suggest password spraying.

events.name: A member was added to a security-enabled universal group.
events.plain: An account was added to a domain (universal) security group.
events.why: Additions to groups like Enterprise Admins give control across the whole forest. Check every one.

events.name: SID History was added to an account.
events.plain: An account was given the identity of another account from a migration (SID History).
events.why: Can secretly give an account admin rights. Microsoft rates this event high: one occurrence is worth checking.

events.name: A user account was unlocked.
events.plain: A locked-out account was unlocked.
events.why: Match it to the 4740 lockout and a help-desk request.

events.name: A Kerberos authentication ticket (TGT) was requested.
events.plain: On a domain controller: an account asked for a Kerberos ticket-granting ticket, the first step of a domain sign-in.
events.why: Failures and requests from odd places or with weak encryption types can point to password attacks or forged tickets.

events.name: A Kerberos service ticket was requested.
events.plain: On a domain controller: an account asked for a ticket to use a specific service.
events.why: Many requests for service accounts with weak (RC4) encryption can mean Kerberoasting.

events.name: Kerberos pre-authentication failed.
events.plain: On a domain controller: a Kerberos sign-in failed, often because of a wrong password.
events.why: Many failures across many accounts suggest password spraying against the domain.

events.name: The computer attempted to validate the credentials for an account.
events.plain: A computer checked a username and password using NTLM (the older Windows sign-in method).
events.why: Failures in bulk suggest password guessing; NTLM use where Kerberos is expected can mean pass-the-hash.

events.name: A session was reconnected to a Window Station.
events.plain: Someone reconnected to an existing session, usually a Remote Desktop session.
events.why: Shows Remote Desktop use and the address it came from.

events.name: A session was disconnected from a Window Station.
events.plain: A session was disconnected without signing out, usually a Remote Desktop session.
events.why: With 4778, it gives the timeline of Remote Desktop use.

events.name: The name of an account was changed.
events.plain: An account was renamed.
events.why: Renaming an account can disguise it, for example making an attacker's account look like a service account.

events.name: A user's local group membership was enumerated.
events.plain: A program listed which local groups a user belongs to.
events.why: Often normal, but bursts from unusual programs can be an attacker mapping who has admin rights.

events.name: The workstation was locked.
events.plain: The computer was locked.
events.why: Helps show when the user stepped away.

events.name: The workstation was unlocked.
events.plain: The computer was unlocked.
events.why: Helps show when the user came back; failed unlocks show as 4625 with logon type 7.

logonTypes.name: Interactive
logonTypes.plain: Someone signed in at this computer's own keyboard and screen.

logonTypes.name: Network
logonTypes.plain: A user or computer connected over the network, such as to a shared folder.

logonTypes.name: Batch
logonTypes.plain: A scheduled task or batch job ran as this account without a person signing in.

logonTypes.name: Service
logonTypes.plain: A Windows service was started under this account.

logonTypes.name: NetworkCleartext
logonTypes.plain: A network sign-in where the password was sent to Windows unhashed, such as basic authentication to a web server.

logonTypes.name: NewCredentials
logonTypes.plain: A program ran with different credentials for network connections (for example runas /netonly).

logonTypes.name: RemoteInteractive
logonTypes.plain: Someone signed in remotely with Remote Desktop.

logonTypes.name: CachedInteractive
logonTypes.plain: Someone signed in with credentials stored on the computer, without contacting a domain controller.

statusCodes.plain: No logon server was available to check the sign-in.
statusCodes.why: Usually an infrastructure or availability problem, not an attack.

statusCodes.plain: The username does not exist (misspelled or bad user account).
statusCodes.why: Several in a row can mean someone is guessing which usernames exist.

statusCodes.plain: The username exists but the password was wrong.
statusCodes.why: Watch for many in a row, especially on admin or service accounts.
Watch for many in a row, especially on admin or service accounts. The sub status often gives the exact reason.

statusCodes.plain: The sign-in was outside the hours this account is allowed to sign in.
The sign-in came from a workstation this account is not allowed to use.
The account has not been granted this kind of sign-in (logon right) on this computer.
The Netlogon service was not started.
statusCodes.why: Usually an infrastructure or availability problem, not an attack.

statusCodes.plain: An authentication firewall protects this computer and the account is not allowed to sign in to it.
